title: Spec browser
summary: A `.spec` folder says what the code is meant to do. The app lets you read it.
description:
Code says what a program does, not what it was meant to do. A repository's `.spec` folder holds that: one JSON file per part of the product, all following one schema, next to the pictures they show.

The folders are the outline. An item's id is its path without `.spec/` and `.json`, and a folder's own item is its `index.json`.

requirements.text: Every `.json` file in `.spec` is one item. Every other file is an asset.
All items follow one schema, published as `schema/spec.schema.json`. The file is generated from the schema the app reads with, and a test fails when they differ.
A file that can't be read (not JSON, an unknown key, a missing title) is listed as a problem with the reason. The rest of the spec still shows.
A figure that isn't in the folder, a related id that leads nowhere and a requirement id used twice anywhere in the spec are listed as problems.

history.text: A figure that isn't in the folder, a related id that leads nowhere and a requirement id used twice are listed as problems.
history.reason: Requirement ids became unique in the whole spec, not just in their item.

requirements.text: A spec's size doesn't matter. One request finds the folder and one lists its files; their contents are read in batches, by git object id, only for what is being looked at. A spec of up to 300 items is read whole.

history.text: The whole folder loads in one request, so moving between items never waits.
history.reason: Reading the whole folder in one request put a ceiling on a spec's size and on how deep it could nest.

requirements.text: The outline can be filtered by the words in titles, summaries, descriptions and requirements. A matching requirement opens its item with that requirement highlighted.
The spec of any branch can be browsed, and links inside it stay on that branch.
A path under an item's code opens that file or folder in the app.

deprecation.reason: Items no longer list code files. A spec says what the product does and isn't tied to any code base, so the format has no field that points into one.

requirements.text: A repository whose default branch has a spec shows a way into it on its overview.
Items nest as deep as the folders do.

history.text: Items can be nested three folders deep. A deeper folder is listed as a problem.
history.reason: The limit of three folders came from reading the folder in one request of fixed depth. Listing the files first removed it.

requirements.text: A repository's menu, a branch without a spec and the list of a spec's problems each offer a prompt for a coding agent to write the spec or improve it. The prompt stands on its own: it includes the schema, the current outline and the problems.
An item that is listed but not read yet shows under its file's name, and is never reported as a problem.
Long lists show 100 rows at a time. Filtering reads the whole spec once and says how far it is.
A file's contents are read once per run of the app, whichever branches it is on, and forgotten on sign-out.

Requirement ids are unique in the whole spec, so a requirement can be referred to by its id alone: `#S15` in `related` finds it in whichever item it is. In a spec too large to read whole, ids are checked among the items read so far.

A requirement or item that is no longer wanted is kept, with the status `deprecated` and a `deprecation` giving the reason and optionally what replaced it and when. The status without the record, or the record without the status, is listed as a problem.
Deprecated requirements are folded away below the live ones, shown with why they were dropped, and not counted among the requirements. They are still found by the filter.
`spec-llms.txt` at the root of this repository describes the format for coding agents. It is generated from the same text as the agent prompt, and a test fails when it is stale.

A requirement has a version, 1 by default. Its earlier versions are kept in its `history`, oldest first, each with what it said and the reason it was replaced. A version that doesn't match the length of the history, or a history out of order, is listed as a problem.
A requirement with earlier versions shows its version, and unfolds to its history, newest first. The filter finds a requirement by what it used to say and by why it changed.
A reference can name a version of a requirement, as `#S19@1`. A version the requirement hasn't reached leads nowhere.
The format has nothing that points into a code base: no field for files or paths. An item that still has the old `code` list is read without it, and listed as a problem that says to remove it.

figures.alt: An item in the spec browser, with its requirements, a figure, code and related items
figures.caption: An item: status, requirements, pictures, and where it lives in the code.

questions: Should a pull request show which items its changed files belong to, from each item's `code`?
Should requirements name the tests that prove them?
Guests can't browse a spec: reading the folder in one request needs GitHub's GraphQL API, which needs a token. Worth a slower path over REST?
